pages.text:
LOCALLY LED FINANCE FOR NATURE
6
Summary 
Biodiversity loss is one of the most urgent crises affecting our planet. Species extinction rates are higher than ever 
before in human history, with over a million plant and animal species expected to become extinct over the coming 
decades if no action is taken (IPBES, 2019). To address this problem, financial flows will need to be redirected and 
reconfigured to move our economic activities away from activities that harm nature (such as deforestation, agricultural 
expansion and mining), and towards activities that benefit and restore nature (such as conservation, agroforestry and 
agroecology). Nature finance is therefore essential to halt and reverse the biodiversity loss crisis.
The Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) includes two ambitious targets on nature finance (Targets 18 and 19) that 
seek to close the US$700 billion biodiversity funding gap — including to raise US$200 billion of new finance per year 
and redirect US$500 billion of harmful subsidies per year by 2030. However, the existing funding vehicles established 
to channel this finance, such as the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund (GBFF) and the Cali Fund, have so far not 
delivered at the scale required. Furthermore, the targets lack attention to how much finance will reach the communities 
who live closest to nature around the world and who possess the best knowledge and skills to protect it, especially 
Indigenous Peoples (IPs) and local communities (LCs).
Crucially, for nature finance to meet the needs of these communities, be rights-based and be effective at halting 
and restoring nature, projects must be led by local actors rather than just implemented alongside them but designed 
externally. The principles for locally led adaptation (LLA) and the principles for inclusive nature action (INA) provide 
valuable frameworks to guide nature finance funders and policymakers on how to channel locally led finance. While 
these principles have received wide endorsement in policy spaces, evidence on how much nature finance actually aligns 
with these principles, and is locally led, is lacking.
In this report, we explore trends in international nature finance flows to estimate how much is implemented with local 
actors and how much is locally led. ‘Locally led’ and ‘locally implemented’ funding are considered here not as the same 
thing but as distinct concepts; funding can be implemented at the local level without being driven by the priorities 
of local actors or implemented by them directly. Locally implemented nature action is usually designed by external 
stakeholders rather than the communities themselves and so can still miss the mark in terms of meeting the needs 
of local actors and ensuring they have agency to design and implement projects in their own way. On the other hand, 
nature action that is locally led ensures local actors play a leading role in the design, implementation, decision making 
and governance of nature projects (see Box 3). This nuance is important for understanding the type of impact nature 
finance is able to effect. In a similar way, this report also offers reflections on the distinction between nature and climate 
finance that is made at the international policy level. For local actors, for whom the impacts and lived experiences of 
nature loss and climate change may be indistinguishable, focusing on the different categories of finance is artificial 
and often meaningless. Better outcomes can be achieved for both nature and climate if finance is ultimately locally led, 
supporting local priorities without artificial separations.
As well as eliciting the difference between locally implemented and locally led nature finance, we further distinguish 
between nature finance implemented with IPs and finance that is Indigenous led, given that conflating IPs with other local 
actors often obscures how little funding targets or reaches IPs specifically. Despite our efforts here, it is important to note 
that although ‘locally led’ is an advancement of ‘locally implemented’, it still does not adequately capture the full asks of IPs. 
Going beyond implementing or leading projects designed to take place within their territories, they instead ask for projects 
to actually support their own self-determined priorities in accordance with their own processes, needs and responsibilities 
to nature.
While efforts have been made previously to calculate the amount of funding reaching the local level, we did not find any 
existing studies that aimed to determine how much nature finance is locally led (as opposed to locally implemented, or 
targeting the local level in some way). This analysis uses a keyword search methodology adapted from a previous study 
by Treichel et al. in 2025 (see Box 1).

SUMMARY

Box 1. Studies that informed this research
The study by Treichel et al. (2025) is foundational for this report; it in turn leant on the approaches by Soanes et al. 
in 2017 and Watkiss et al. in 2023. 
Treichel et al. analysed flows of climate finance to the local level using the Organisation for Economic Co-operation 
and Development’s Development Assistance Committee’s (OECD DAC) Climate-Related Development Finance 
(CRDF) data and applied a keyword search methodology to funding tagged with the climate-related Rio markers. 
The Treichel et al. study found that 29% of the climate finance descriptions and titles include some reference to 
local implementation and 0.17% of finance mentions locally led climate action.
In this report, we adapt the methodology and apply it to the OECD DAC official development assistance (ODA) data 
marked with the Rio marker for biodiversity over 2011–2024.
Our key findings show that, of the ODA reported to the OECD DAC between 2021 and 2024 tagged for biodiversity:
	
•	 33.7% of the funding line descriptions or titles include some reference to the local level, with only 
0.28% referring to ‘locally led’,1 and
	
•	 2.24% include some reference to ‘Indigenous Peoples’ or other related keywords, with only 0.001% 
referring to ‘Indigenous led’.
Figure 1 illustrates how small a proportion of overall nature finance even includes any mention of local implementation 
or local actors and how extremely tiny the proportion is that is locally or Indigenous led. It also demonstrates how 
data constraints limit our ability to accurately estimate total funding amounts flowing to local actors, which would fall 
somewhere in between.

pages.text:
LOCALLY LED FINANCE FOR NATURE
8
The findings are deeply concerning, as they indicate that even where money is spent at the local level, or there are 
benefits for local actors, over 99% of nature projects are still led by non-local actors. IPs and LCs who steward nature 
may still lack decision making power and agency over how funding is spent in their territories. While nature finance 
with some local implementation is increasing, the results reveal that almost 70% of all biodiversity funding included no 
reference to the local level at all.
Furthermore, within the nature finance that refers to local implementation, we found that only 2.89% mention the 
specific term ‘Indigenous Peoples’ and 6.64% mention any keywords related to ‘Indigenous’. We can conclude, 
therefore, that most (more than 90%) local-level funding goes to non-Indigenous actors. The term ‘Indigenous led’ was 
only found six times in around 233,000 funding lines over 2011–2024, indicating that leadership of IPs is still barely 
recognised in nature finance. This suggests that the vast majority of finance implemented with IPs is still designed and 
led externally.
We also discuss how nature finance is delivered, including the sources of finance, the financial instruments used and 
the trends in commitment versus disbursement data (how much finance is ‘committed’ by donors through pledges or 
other agreements, versus how much is actually dispensed). The United States was found to be the second largest 
funder for projects using ‘locally led’ search terms. Since the vast majority of US funding over 2011–2024 was provided 
via the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), the withdrawal of USAID funding in 2025 means 
that we can reasonably expect to see funding for locally led nature action plummet from 2025 onwards. Preliminary 
data on 2025 figures from the OECD DAC suggests that overall, ODA has declined significantly from 2024, with many 
other funders also reducing their contributions (OECD, 2026). This can be expected to have a damaging impact on 
nature finance, including finance to the local level and finance that is either Indigenous or locally led.
The Global Environment Facility (GEF) — the primary multilateral fund delivering nature finance and host of the flagship 
financial mechanism of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), the GBFF — was found to provide only 1.65% of 
total reported nature finance. However, there is a particular methodological challenge related to the way GEF funding 
is reported to the OECD DAC, which means this is likely an underestimate. It is too early to assess the impact of the 
GBFF on biodiversity or local-level funding since it only began operating in 2023 and disbursement data is not yet 
available via the OECD DAC data that we use as our source.
On the intersection between nature finance and climate finance, we argue that separating climate and nature finance 
streams matters for ‘upstream’ accounting discussions to track progress against the different goals of the Rio 
conventions2 and to hold funders to account for their financial commitments to ensure funds are not double-counted. 
However, this separation can be actively harmful for its effectiveness ‘downstream’, since it can lead to projects being 
designed with limited scope, or worse, to the exclusion of the needs of key actors on the ground, in whose name such 
funding is provided in the first place. Efforts should be made in international policy to break down the siloes between 
nature and climate and streamline local-level finance for these issues under unified funding channels.
The report concludes with several recommendations for nature finance policymakers and funding bodies, as well as 
recommendations for further research. These include:
	
•	
 More finance for nature needs to reach the local level and more needs to be locally led. Additionally, more 
finance for nature needs to reach IPs and be led by IPs.
	
•	
 Specific indicators should be introduced to the OECD DAC and other reporting frameworks, such as the GBF 
monitoring framework and GEF indicators for the GBFF, to accurately measure how much finance reaches 
local actors and how much is locally led. Within the OECD DAC reporting, a first step would be to expand the 
existing channel of delivery codes to allow subcategories to clearly distinguish between local funding recipients 
based in funder countries from those in recipient countries. In addition, funders should engage in substantive 
dialogue with IPs to assess the extent to which projects are in line with the priorities of IPs and to explore the 
development of appropriate tracking mechanisms.
2 The Rio conventions refer to the three separate UN conventions established in 1992 at the Rio Earth Summit to address the interconnected challenges of climate 
change, biodiversity loss and desertification. The three conventions are: the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the Convention on 
Biological Diversity (CBD) and the UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD). See more here: https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-rio-conventions

pages.text:
SUMMARY
   9
	
•	
 International policy debates should focus more attention on bilateral funding sources as they currently dominate 
the nature finance landscape. There is currently an over-emphasis on the multilateral funds, especially the GEF, 
in nature finance policy discussions, which diminishes the responsibility of funder countries, especially in terms 
of the provision of grant/concessional finance for nature.
	
•	
 In response to the withdrawal of large amounts of USAID funding, all funders should increase their focus on 
delivering more locally led finance for nature. This is now needed more than ever and there is potential for small 
changes to have a significant impact.
	
•	
 The GEF, as the key multilateral funder channelling funding to deliver the GBF targets, should focus on meeting 
the target of getting 20% of funds to IPs and LCs within the GBFF and apply this across its wider funding 
portfolio.
	
•	
 The use of debt instruments for nature finance should be minimised. Where they are used, they should be 
designed in ways that ensure the finance reaches the local level and can be locally led. They must respect the 
rights and values of IPs and LCs, with full adherence to self-determination and free, prior and informed consent 
(FPIC) processes.
	
•	
 Funder countries should collectively agree upon consistent reporting approaches to ensure transparent and 
consistent tracking of their funding commitments. Efforts should be made to streamline this process to avoid 
double counting and to reduce ‘over-tagging’ of projects with the Rio markers.
	
•	
 Policy negotiations on finance within the CBD and United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change 
(UNFCCC) should aim to channel nature and climate finance through joint funding streams to ensure finance 
addresses both issues holistically.
We urge parties to the CBD negotiations on resource mobilisation, financial mechanism and the monitoring framework to 
consider these recommendations and address them at the 2026 UN Biodiversity Conference (CBD COP17) and beyond.

LOCALLY LED FINANCE FOR NATURE
10     
1	
 
Introduction
Biodiversity loss is one of the most urgent crises affecting our planet. Species extinction rates are higher than ever 
before in human history, with over a million plant and animal species expected to become extinct over the coming 
decades if no action is taken (IPBES, 2019). Many of the Earth’s valuable ecosystems are at risk of collapse, with 
severe consequences for the natural resources we depend on to sustain human life. Without nature, the food, water and 
air we rely on will disappear. However, international funding to conserve these natural resources falls far short of what is 
needed and the extent to which the funding provided reaches local communities remains unverified.
The causes of biodiversity loss are complex and varied, ranging from overconsumption and extraction of natural 
resources, changes in land and sea use for agriculture and urbanisation, climate change, pollution, and invasive species 
(UNEP, 2023a). The solutions to these issues are similarly complex and require a multisectoral response. However, 
one thing that is clear is that financial flows will need to be redirected and reconfigured to move our economic activities 
away from activities that harm nature (such as deforestation, agricultural expansion and mining) and towards activities 
that benefit and restore nature (such as conservation, agroforestry and agroecology).
Nature finance is essential to halt and reverse the biodiversity loss crisis. In this report, we define ‘nature finance’ as 
finance that is beneficial for nature and biodiversity: the flow of funds from all sources to conserve biodiversity, ecosystems 
and species and support positive outcomes for people.3 Nature finance is closely related to climate finance (which refers 
to finance for climate mitigation, adaptation and loss and damage), with many of the same funders and recipients used for 
international nature finance and international climate finance, often also using similar types of governance mechanisms to 
manage and track their flows. However, they can also be administered, implemented and sometimes generated differently 
because they relate to two different Rio conventions: CBD and UNFCCC. While most nature finance also has positive 
benefits for climate, the opposite is not always true. Nonetheless, we acknowledge that the distinction between ‘nature 
finance’ and ‘climate finance’ outside of international policy discussions can seem artificial — and often meaningless — for 
local communities experiencing the direct impacts of these issues. In this report, we explore trends in international nature 
finance flows and advocate for synergistic finance that addresses both nature and climate holistically.
1.1 The current state of nature finance policy and practice
The GBF (CBD, no date) is the global policy instrument that aims to address all aspects of biodiversity loss and 
achieve the vision of living in harmony with nature by 2050. It was adopted in December 2022 by parties to the CBD 
at CBD COP15. Within it, there are two ambitious targets on nature finance (Targets 18 and 19) that seek to close 
the US$700 billion biodiversity funding gap — including aiming to raise US$200 billion of new finance per year and 
redirect US$500 billion of harmful subsidies per year by 2030.
Several flagship funds for nature have been established since the agreement of the GBF, including the GBFF, the Cali 
Fund and the Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF). However, pledges to these funds have remained far behind target 
so far: the latest contributions to the GBFF total US$383.96 million (World Bank, no date), the Cali Fund has received 
3 See IIED’s full definition of nature finance in the 2025–2030 nature finance strategy here: www.iied.org/22665iied

INTRODUCTION
  11
one donation of just US$1,000 (Chandrasekhar and Dwyer, 2025) and the TFFF has secured US$6.7 billion (Carla 
Ruas, 2025), less than a quarter of what is required to fully operationalise the fund. These contributions fall far short of 
the GBF target to raise US$200 billion per year for nature.
While raising new finance for nature is important, it is only half of the story. GBF commitments are focused on national 
levels, but biodiversity loss impacts are felt locally, especially by IPs and LCs. These are the people who steward nature 
globally and possess the best knowledge and skills to protect it. There is compelling evidence that nature is best 
conserved when it is managed by IPs and LCs, including local actors such as smallholder farmers and fishers and 
pastoralists (IPBES, 2019; Fa et al., 2020; Dawson et al., 2021; Dawson et al., 2024). Even more important than raising 
new finance, therefore, is to ensure that the finance we already have is reaching these groups; and any new finance 
raised will only be effective if it is channelled in the same way.
What is missing from the GBF targets is the aim to channel finance directly to IPs and LCs. The GBFF, Cali Fund and 
TFFF all include a target to direct 20% of their funding to IPs and LCs, but it is unclear how this is being implemented 
or monitored. Previous tracking studies have been unable to determine how much funding from the GEF reaches 
IPs and LCs (Sorsby et al., 2025). Furthermore, the targets do not specify that the funding must reach Indigenous or 
local organisations directly, meaning in many cases funding can pass to an international agency or nongovernmental 
organisation (NGO) and still fulfil the criteria provided that the project intends to deliver benefits for IPs and LCs. 
Clearer and more explicit targets to ensure that funding is put directly into the hands of Indigenous and local 
organisations and for them to have full control over allocation of resources and decision making, are still lacking.
1.2 Locally led nature action
Securing direct access to funding has been a key priority for IPs and LCs within global policy for many decades, 
both for nature and climate finance. The LLA principles were developed in 2021 in response to calls from the Least 
Developed Countries for international climate adaptation finance to reach the countries most vulnerable to climate 
change directly (IIED, no date-a). LLA principle 3 specifically calls for patient and predictable funding that can be 
accessed more easily (see Box 2). The LLA principles also call for decision making to be devolved to the lowest 
appropriate level (principle 1). This is a key distinction; for funding to be truly locally led, it must not only reach the local 
level, but local actors must also have agency to decide how funding is spent.
The LLA principles have gained traction in policy and have been endorsed by more than 150 organisations. LLA is 
now mentioned in the Global Goal on Adaptation and several multilateral funders have opened funding windows or 
adopted frameworks specifically designed to deliver LLA, including the Adaptation Fund and the Green Climate Fund. 
Nonetheless, the principles do not include a clear reference to protecting nature as a prerequisite to climate adaptation.
Box 2. Principles for locally led adaptation
1.	 Devolving decision making to the lowest appropriate level
2.	 Addressing structural inequalities faced by women, youth, children, disabled and displaced people, Indigenous 
Peoples and marginalised ethnic groups
3.	 Providing patient and predictable funding that can be accessed more easily
4.	 Investing in local capabilities to leave an institutional legacy
5.	 Building a robust understanding of climate risk and uncertainty
6.	 Flexible programming and learning
7.	 Ensuring transparency and accountability
8.	 Collaborative action and investment

pages.text:
LOCALLY LED FINANCE FOR NATURE
12
In response to this, a new set of INA principles emerged in 2024 (IIED, no date-b), drawing on the LLA principles 
and the Shandia principles developed by the Global Alliance of Territorial Communities (no date). The INA principles 
include greater emphasis on the inclusion of IPs and gender-responsive, rights-based approaches and were developed 
specifically with locally led nature action in mind. INA principle 5 calls for direct, patient, flexible, predictable and 
accessible funding to reach IPs and LCs (see Box 3). They also call for devolving decision making and strengthening 
local leadership (principle 2), similarly to LLA.
Box 3. Principles for inclusive nature action
1.	 Recognise and respect rights
2.	 Devolve decision making and strengthen local leadership
3.	 Recognise and address structural and intersectional inequalities
4.	 Encourage flexible, adaptive biodiversity programming
5.	 Provide direct, patient, flexible, predictable and accessible funding
6.	 Recognise the mutual value of scientific and local and traditional knowledge
7.	 Promote collaborative and coherent action and investment
8.	 Safeguard local actors, beyond ‘do no harm’
1.3 Locally led versus locally implemented
In this report, we consider ‘locally led’ funding as distinct from ‘locally implemented’ funding, or funding that is simply 
targeted towards the local level (see Box 4 for an explanation of what we mean by ‘local’ and related terms). For funding 
to be locally led, there must be evidence that it not only reaches local actors such as IPs and LCs, but that they are actively 
leading the project and have the authority to make decisions over funding allocations and project decisions. Only in this 
way can funding be in line with the LLA and INA principles.
In this report, we advocate for ‘locally led nature action’ and ‘Indigenous-led nature action’ over nature action that is only 
implemented with local actors or IPs. This is because IPs and LCs must lead the design and implementation of projects 
in order for nature finance to be rights-based and impactful, rather than just implementing projects that have been 
designed externally.
We acknowledge that neither ‘locally led’ nor ‘Indigenous led’ terms are able to fully capture the essence of what IPs 
have been asking for, which is for finance to support projects that are needed and wanted by communities, in line with 
their self-determined needs and priorities.
1.4 Existing work tracking nature finance
To date, several studies have attempted to quantify the amount of nature finance that is currently available globally. The 
2020 Financing Nature Report estimated global conservation finance in 2019 at US$124 billion to US$143 billion and 
found an annual shortfall of US$711 billion in the amount needed to reverse the decline in biodiversity by 2030 (Deutz et 
al., 2020). The OECD Comprehensive Overview of Global Biodiversity Finance (2020) found that average global spending 
on biodiversity between 2015 and 2017 was between US$78 billion and US$91 billion per year, but governments spend 
five to six times more than this (approximately US$500 billion per year) on nature‑harming activities (OECD, 2020). The 
State of Finance for Nature report series by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) measures total finance 
flows to nature-based solutions, finding that in 2023 that these were roughly US$220 billion; a figure that is dwarfed 
by the amount of nature-harmful finance at a ratio of more than 30:1 (UNEP, 2026). The Biodiversity Finance Trends 
report by The Nature Conservancy analysed financial flows against the GBF targets and found that while overall finance 
for nature is increasing, we are still not on track to bridge the US$700 billion funding gap by 2030 (Biodiversity Finance 
Trends, 2025). Gonon et al. (2024) summarise the set of funding assessment studies published so far and call for a new 
approach that goes beyond quantification of nature finance to a wider reform of the financial system to improve access to 
finance for low- and middle-income countries and address socioeconomic and justice challenges.

INTRODUCTION
  13
Box 4. What do we mean by ‘local’?
Earlier studies have defined ‘local’ institutions as both formal and informal organisations that operate at sub-national 
level (Soanes et al., 2021; Treichel et al., 2025; Patel, 2024). Local actors can therefore include:
	
• 	 Public entities: subnational authorities and governments that are responsible for meeting local needs
	
• 	 Private entities: formal and informal enterprises
	
• 	 Civil society: community-based organisations, IPs organisations, local groups and social movements, and
	
•	
Households and individuals: those that share administrative units, a sense of community, locality or 
shocks and stresses.
Our definition of ‘local’ is similar to the OECD’s working definition (OECD, 2024d), which includes actors who are 
based in and centred on local issues, subject to local laws and operating within the local context. While both our 
definition and the OECD’s definition exclude international NGOs and their country offices, multilateral organisations 
and international private-sector organisations, a key distinction is that, unlike the OECD, our definition excludes 
national governments. We consider ‘local’ to imply communities or connected groups of people who are likely to 
have shared experiences of climate and nature impacts (Rahman et al., 2023).
In particular, we recognise IPs as important rights holders for locally led action on nature and aim to distinguish 
activities led, directed and implemented by IPs from those at the general community level. In sum, we use the 
following definitions in this report to distinguish between the different types of ‘local level’ nature finance:
	
•	
Nature action implemented with local actors: biodiversity actions that involve community members 
as beneficiaries or that are implemented at the local level. This includes funding that targets a specific 
community, or is spent within that community, but is not necessarily driven by the priorities of local actors or 
implemented by them directly. Locally implemented nature action is usually designed by external stakeholders 
rather than the communities themselves.
	
•	
Locally led nature action: biodiversity actions that give decision-making power to the community in 
question and broadly align with the LLA and INA principles. Funding for locally led nature action would not 
only reach local actors directly, they would also play a leading role in the design, implementation, decision 
making and governance of nature projects.
	
•	
Nature action implemented with IPs: biodiversity actions that involve IPs as beneficiaries or are 
implemented with IPs. This includes funding that targets IPs, or is spent within their territories, but is not 
necessarily driven by their priorities or implemented by them directly. Nature action implemented with IPs is 
usually designed by external stakeholders rather than by Indigenous communities themselves.
	
•	
Indigenous-led nature action: biodiversity actions that give decision-making power to IPs and broadly 
align with the LLA and INA principles, including to respect self-determination, land rights and FPIC 
processes. Funding for Indigenous-led nature action would not only reach IPs directly, but they would also 
play a leading role in the design, implementation, decision making and governance of nature projects.
Fewer studies have aimed to quantify flows of nature finance reaching the local level. The Path to Scale funding 
dashboard is one existing initiative in this area that consolidates and presents data on funding available for IPs, LCs 
and Afro-descendant Peoples specifically for land tenure and forest guardianship (Path to Scale, no date). The State of 
Funding for Tenure Rights report complements this initiative and finds that funding for tenure rights is less than 1% of 
all climate aid (Rights and Resources Initiative and Rainforest Foundation Norway, 2025). The 2024 report ‘Money well 
spent?’ (Family Farmers for Climate Action, 2024) concluded that only around 14% of funding from the GEF and GCF 
is targeted at activities relevant to smallholder farmers, and a previous IIED study found that nature finance from the 
GEF is not effectively reaching local actors, IPs or LCs (Sorsby et al., 2025). The OECD Biodiversity and Development 
Finance report estimates the share of biodiversity-related official development financing (ODF) targeting IPs and LCs at 
6% of OECD DAC members’ total biodiversity-related ODF in 2022 (OECD, 2024a).

LOCALLY LED FINANCE FOR NATURE
14
These existing studies offer a helpful foundation for our analysis. While efforts have been made previously to calculate 
the amount of funding reaching the local level, no existing study was found that aimed to determine how much nature 
finance is locally led (as opposed to locally implemented, or targeting the local level in some way). Our research is also 
focused on ODA — that is, on ‘development aid’ — rather than ODF. ODF goes beyond ODA and also includes non-
concessional development resources and other official flows (OOF) that do not meet the criteria to be considered 
development aid, such as export credits or loans provided at market rates.
The present study aims to complement the existing research in this area by analysing the full set of development aid 
data from the OECD DAC tagged with the Rio marker for biodiversity to estimate (1) how much nature-focused ODA 
is reaching the local level and (2) how much nature-focused ODA is locally led. We also aim to estimate how much 
nature‑focused ODA is going to IPs specifically, as important rights holders for local action on nature, and how much 
nature-focused ODA is Indigenous led. The study also offers some insights into nature finance reaching urban areas 
and the sources and types of nature finance, and offers reflections on the relationship between locally led nature 
finance and locally led climate finance.
This report builds directly on the methodology used by Treichel et al. in 2025. That study analysed the OECD DAC’s 
CRDF data and found that 29% of climate finance includes some reference to local implementation and 0.17% of 
funding mentions locally led climate action. The actual amount of funding reaching the local level is unknowable from 
the data available. In this report, we adapt the methodology and apply it to the OECD DAC ODA data marked with the 
Rio marker for biodiversity.
We use a keyword search methodology adapted from similar prior studies (Treichel et al., 2025; OECD, 2024a; Sorsby 
et al., 2025). Crucially, we look only at ODA finance and not at other investments that are non-ODA. As a result, our 
findings are limited to OECD DAC member countries. For consistency with previous studies, we look at nature finance 
from 2011–2024 to observe trends over time. We also offer early insights into how locally led nature finance differs 
from locally led climate finance, as per the results found by Treichel et al. in 2025, noting the two studies are not directly 
comparable for reasons outlined in Section 3.3.2.
The remainder of this report is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines our methodology and limitations, Section 3 
presents our results and a discussion of the findings and Section 4 presents recommendations for nature finance 
policymakers and funding bodies.

Methodology
This research applied a keyword search on all biodiversity-relevant ODA reported to the OECD DAC over 2011–2014. 
The approach replicates work already done on climate-related ODA, using an expanded set of nature-relevant 
keywords. We used simple coding via Python to help refine the very large datasets and run the search, and then Excel 
to undertake the analysis. Our research highlights some of the benefits and limitations of this approach.
The research involved two concurrent steps (outlined below) to generate an Excel spreadsheet of results that displays the 
number of keywords found in the titles and descriptions of funding lines reported to the OECD DAC as ODA. A third step was 
needed to refine the Excel output such that the figures more accurately reflect whether the funding lines in question were 
primarily about biodiversity and to exclude non-ODA; this Excel output was then analysed to create the research findings. To 
do this, we followed the same basic approach outlined by Treichel et al. in 2025 (see that publication’s Appendix 1. Detailed 
methodology), which in turn leant on the approaches by Soanes et al. in 2017 and Watkiss et al. in 2023:
First, we sourced and refined the best available dataset. The OECD DAC does not produce an equivalent set 
of data for biodiversity projects to the CRDF dataset used in Treichel et al. (2025). OECD DAC colleagues helped to 
identify the most appropriate dataset for this purpose: the parquet-format dataset marked as ‘CRS: Creditor Reporting 
System (flows)’ within the ODA data available from the OECD Data Explorer (OECD, no date).
This dataset includes all development aid going back to 1973 and so is very large. Using Python, we reduced the 
parquet-formatted dataset to only include data from 2011 onwards and only that marked for biodiversity — in other 
words, only the rows marked with a ‘1’ (significant) or a ‘2’ (principal) in the biodiversity column (see more on this 
below). This produced a refined dataset on which to apply our keyword search.
Second, we expanded, refined, tested and finalised our keyword search terms and associated search code. 
To define our set of keywords, we used the keywords from Treichel et al. (2025) as a starting point. This list was 
supplemented with additional keywords relevant for nature and biodiversity finance, as well as keywords used in other pieces 
of biodiversity-finance focused work. These include the draft OECD DAC publication Biodiversity and Development Finance 
2015–2023 (not yet published) and IIED’s GEF-focused research report into funding estimates to IPs, LCs and women and 
girls (Sorsby et al., 2025), as well as the GEF Independent Evaluation Office (IEO)’s Evaluation of GEF Engagement with 
Indigenous Peoples (GEF IEO, 2018). The set of keywords, including the most appropriate French and Spanish equivalents 
(as the two other most commonly used reporting languages to the OECD DAC) and the ideal ‘stem’ words, were refined 
through testing. The final list of keywords across three languages — English, French and Spanish — is shown in Appendix 1.
We then updated the code to suit this new set of keywords and ran the keyword search code on the downloaded and 
refined dataset produced via step 1. The code produces an Excel file that replicates the columns used by the OECD 
DAC, with an additional column for each keyword. Each additional column displays the associated number of keywords 
found within the ‘project title’ and ‘long_description’ columns for that row. The code is available here: https://github.
com/entaylor/RioMarkersKeywords.
This produced an Excel spreadsheet of around 233,000 funding lines covering the period 2011–2024 that were marked 
as either ‘significant’ or ‘principal’ for the biodiversity marker — in other words, with either a ‘1’ or a ‘2’ in the ‘biodiversity’ 
column. The Rio markers are a way for those reporting their funding to indicate the degree to which they align with each

of the three Rio conventions. They are designed to identify whether the Rio ‘issue’ in question — in this case, biodiversity 
— is the principal (primary) or a significant (secondary) objective of an activity, or if the activity does not target biodiversity 
at all (OECD, 2024b). Funding that is not principally or primarily for that purpose is then discounted to reflect that it is less 
directly relevant. Following the approach of the OECD DAC in their reporting on nature finance in their Biodiversity and 
Development Finance 2015–2022 publication (OECD, 2024a), we applied a 40% coefficient on data coded as having a 
significant biodiversity objective (using code 1) and a coefficient of 100% on data coded as having a principal biodiversity 
objective (using code 2). We applied 0% for funding not targeted or not screened.
Third, the Excel output was then further refined following Treichel et al.’s detailed methodology to apply funding 
coefficients based on the Rio marker and to exclude non-ODA:
	
•	
 We applied the relevant Rio marker coefficients based on the score in the ‘biodiversity’ column to the 
‘usd_disbursement_defl’ column (in other words, to funding disbursements). The resulting funding amounts 
were displayed in a new column called ‘RESULTS (USD)’. To allow comparison between commitment and 
disbursement data (see Section 2.1, below), we repeated this step on the commitments data — we applied the 
relevant Rio marker coefficients based on the ‘biodiversity’ column to the ‘usd_commitment_defl’ column, with 
the results displayed in a new column called ‘COMMITMENT RESULTS_USD’. Throughout this report, we use 
disbursement data as the default, but this additional step allows us to compare the two sets of funding amounts.
	
•	
 Using the ‘category’ column, we excluded all non-ODA flow types (OOF, export credits, private philanthropic 
flows and so on), leaving only code 10 (ODA). In this research, we include all OECD DAC members as eligible 
contributor and recipient countries. Because the data was filtered to only include ODA flows, this meant we did 
not need to exclude any contributor or recipient countries from the dataset.
	
•	
 Using the ‘sector_code’ column, we excluded any remaining non-ODA-relevant activities: General Budget 
Support (510), Action Relating to Debt (600), Administrative Costs of Donors (910), Refugees in Donor 
Countries (930) and Development Awareness (998).
The results in the new column ‘RESULTS (USD)’ were then analysed according to the various available categories 
of information and particularly in terms of the degree to which the frequency of keywords meant that the projects in 
question could be considered locally implemented or locally led.
Note that because each funding line can include more than one keyword, individual keyword funding totals cannot be added.
2.1 Assumptions
For the purposes of this research, we consider ‘nature finance’ to include both funding (that is, grants) and finance 
(in other words, debt instruments) that have been reported to the OECD DAC and marked with the Rio marker for 
biodiversity. We only consider ODA as it is the category of concessional development assistance that most people 
would call ‘aid’ (OECD, 2024b). We therefore do not include OOF or ODF.
In this research, we use the OECD DAC member categories to identify eligible contributor and recipient countries. This differs 
from most climate finance studies, including IIED’s research into funding for LLA (Treichel et al., 2025), which use UNFCCC 
definitions of country categories. This means that all countries remaining after the ‘category’ filter was applied (to exclude 
non-ODA) are included. Note that the EU is an OECD DAC member and treated in the CRS and in this report as bilateral.
The CRS dataset includes both commitment and disbursement data. In this report, we examine disbursement data 
rather than commitment data — that is, we look at how much money OECD DAC members actually gave to countries in 
a given year, rather than how much they committed to countries in that year. Disbursement data seems a more accurate 
set of figures to use to answer the question of how much funding is reaching the local level, but commitment data 
is more commonly used in reporting (see, for example, OECD, 2020; OECD, 2024a) and so our figures may not be 
comparable to other reports. Disbursement data may be less smooth year-on-year, as it will reflect funding transmission 
issues within individual years that are masked by commitment data, but it is more accurate in that it only reflects funding 
that is actually disbursed; commitments that are made but not realised are not included. If commitments were always 
realised, disbursement data would follow very similar patterns to commitment data, with slight lags to reflect the time 
difference between commitments and implementation. As shown in our results section, this is often not the case and so 
we use disbursement data as our default.

2.2 Limitations
There are five key limitations of using the OECD DAC data for our research:
	
•	
First, one consequence of only looking at ODA as reported via the OECD DAC is that we exclude other forms of 
international finance not categorised as development assistance. This means we do not include either private-
sector or philanthropic funding, or other international finance covered by ODF, such as via non-concessional 
loans or export credits. This means our findings may differ from other reports that include ODF. This source of 
data is also not exhaustive and so will not include ‘non-tagged’ nature finance; it also cannot include other flows 
of nature finance not captured through OECD DAC reporting. The purpose of this report is to look at how much 
of the nature-focused development finance provided over the 2011–2024 period targets the local level or is 
locally or Indigenous led.
	
•	
Second, there are well-known limitations to the OECD DAC datasets, particularly around potential over-tagging 
of the Rio markers by funders — that is, funding lines being marked as relevant to the Rio treaties when, in fact, 
they are not (Hicks et al., 2008; Roberts and Weikmans, 2017; Wood and Leng, 2025). This issue has been 
especially well documented for climate; we assume the same tendency applies for biodiversity. This research did 
not attempt to validate the relevance of the funding marked with the Rio marker for biodiversity.
	
•	
Third, this over-tagging leads to questions about the overall accuracy of the OECD DAC data (Doshi and 
Garschagen, 2020; Weikmans et al., 2017). We also did not verify the funding values in the OECD DAC data 
— our focus is on the proportion of funding targeting the local level and for locally led nature action. For this 
purpose, the OECD DAC data provides a relatively robust dataset; but to verify estimates of the total quantity of 
funding provided, this data would need to be compared to other datasets, for example, from end recipients. This 
is beyond the scope of this work; throughout this report we use proportions rather than total funding amounts.
	
•	
Fourth, as outlined in the methodology section above, there is no biodiversity dataset equivalent to the CRDF 
dataset that was used in Treichel et al. (2025). This means that the findings of this research cannot be directly 
compared to that study. We do offer some high-level comparisons between the results in both studies, but 
they are observations on trends only and the different datasets used should be taken into account; the precise 
estimates cannot be compared. We have also compared how many biodiversity projects were also tagged with 
the climate Rio markers, since that speaks to the level of overlap between the two areas of work.
	
•	
Fifth, a further limitation is that the level of detail included in project descriptions in the OECD DAC dataset 
(which together with project titles made up our search fields) can vary enormously from a couple of words to 
several paragraphs; the suitability of using a keyword search on those descriptions obviously varies accordingly.
The keyword search approach also has some known limitations:
	
•	
It is an inherently crude approach, in which the use of various synonyms for ‘local’ acts as a proxy for funding 
reaching the local level. It is widely used (see above examples from the OECD DAC itself, from the GEF IEO 
and from IIED), but there are nevertheless well-known shortcomings. Prime among these is the issue of the 
proportion of the attribution, whereby this approach only allows for the allocation either of all of a funding line if 
synonyms appear, or none of a funding line if they are absent. This all-or-nothing allocation issue severely limits 
the accuracy of any estimations of total funding values made using keyword searches. 
	
•	
It relies on the use of keywords as a proxy for implementation. This relies on a double substitution. First, if a 
concept or keyword is mentioned in an increasing number of funding lines, we take that to indicate an increase 
in funding for that concept or keyword. Second, we take an increase in funding to indicate an increase in 
effective and appropriate implementation. In practice, ideas come in and out of fashion within international aid. 
While the acceptance of ideas may well be demonstrated by increased reference to them, it is important that 
in this report, when we call for increases in funding for particular keywords — especially for locally led and 
Indigenous-led nature action — we are seeking an increase in the effective implementation of those concepts, 
rather than only for increases in funding, and certainly not only for an increase in the use of terminology.

18
	
•	
Selecting keywords to indicate ‘local’ is ambiguous and subjective and open to multiple interpretations of how 
‘local’ is defined. As above, we significantly expanded and refined the keyword list from previous attempts — see 
Appendix 1 for a full list. For example, we expanded the search terms beyond ‘locally led’ and ‘community led’ 
used by Treichel et al. to also include ‘Indigenous led’ in this research, given the unique importance of IPs and 
LCs as nature stewards around the world. We also significantly expanded the French and Spanish translations 
of keywords to capture more of the reported funding. While this process of expanding and refining the keyword 
set has allowed us to improve our approach and increase the accuracy of our searching (as both missed data 
and the number of false positives should be significantly decreased), expanding the set of keywords does 
also open up further questions about how we define ‘local’. For example, terms like ‘gatherer’, ‘hunter’, ‘mother 
earth’, ‘peasant’ and ‘tenure’ would not normally be considered synonyms for ‘local’ in regular conversation. 
However, project descriptions that include these terms are likely to be implemented at the local level. What this 
demonstrates is the complicated nature of what we mean by ‘local’ and the difficulties in accurately drawing 
a boundary around this definition. We have done multiple rounds of testing and review of the words selected, 
and of examining their use in project descriptions to eliminate words that yield too many false positives or are 
otherwise inappropriate, in line with our definition articulated in Box 4, but the philosophical question of what 
counts as local remains (see Jarillo and Barnett, 2021; Panelli and Welch, 2005).
	
•	
A key limitation of this research overall is that we have only performed quantitative analysis on the OECD DAC 
ODA data, but have not gathered inputs from funding recipients. Qualitative data from funding recipients would 
be needed to corroborate the degree to which funded activities genuinely involve local actors or are locally led. 
While this step is beyond the scope of the present study, we acknowledge that the findings can only represent 
a partial picture of where funding really ends up and how. Our methodology also cannot tell us anything about 
the lived experience of implementing nature finance at the local level, to what extent local actors are able to lead 
projects or to what extent projects are in line with, and designed to respond to, the self-determined needs and 
priorities of IPs and LCs.
As a result of these assumptions and limitations, the figures provided should be understood as indicative of funding 
priorities and proportions, rather than a definitive quantum of funding provided.

Results and discussion
This section presents the results of our keyword analysis of OECD DAC nature finance data, including detailed findings 
on how much nature-focused ODA is reaching the local level and how much nature-focused ODA is locally led. We also 
estimate how much nature-focused ODA is going to IPs, as important rights holders for local action on nature, and how 
much nature-focused ODA is Indigenous led.
3.1 Quantities of nature finance
Of the ODA reported to the OECD DAC between 2011 and 2024 tagged for biodiversity, we found that 33.7% 
includes some reference to the local level, with only 0.28% referring to ‘locally led’.4 We found that 2.24% includes 
some reference to ‘Indigenous Peoples’ or other related keywords, with only 0.001% referring to ‘Indigenous led’.
Figure 1 in the summary illustrates how small a proportion of overall nature finance includes any mention of local 
implementation or local actors and how extremely tiny the proportion is that is locally or Indigenous led. It also 
demonstrates the impossibility of estimating how much actually reaches the local level using this data.
3.1.1 Nature finance that is locally led
Only 0.28% of total nature finance over 2011–2024 included ‘locally led’ and its related terms ‘community led’ and 
‘Indigenous led’ (all three terms were searched for with and without hyphens). Even within nature finance that included 
terms that would indicate some local-level implementation, only 0.82% included ‘locally led’ or its related terms. This is an 
extremely low amount, which indicates that local-level implementation does not necessarily amount to a locally led project.
The results show variable use of these terms collectively over time, but with an uptick beginning from 2015 on and then 
a distinct and significant jump from 2023 on (see Figure 2). As outlined in the limitations section, in this report we use 
disbursement figures as the default. The commitment funding shows a similar trend, with the uptick beginning earlier, in 
2022, reaching higher in 2023, but slowing in 2024.
The term ‘community led’ was used in nature finance descriptions as early as 2011 and was used in 54.2% of all 
funding lines that included any of the locally led search terms (making up only 0.15% of all nature finance). ‘Locally 
led’ doesn’t appear until 2017, with increasing use since then. ‘Locally led’ was used in 46.5% of all funding lines that 
included any of the locally led search terms (making up 0.129% of all nature finance). ‘Indigenous led’ was only used in 
six out of the roughly 233,000 total reported nature finance lines — one or two funding lines each in 2019, 2021, 2023 
and 2024 (making up only 0.001% of all nature finance). ‘Indigenous led’ only makes up a tiny fraction of all the locally 
led search terms, with ‘locally led’ and ‘community led’ accounting for over 99% of all references to nature finance with 
local leadership (see more on nature finance to IPs in Section 3.1.4). Note that more than one search term can be used 
in any one funding line, so these percentages may add up to more than 100%.
None of the 24 French and Spanish synonyms we tried for ‘locally led’ and ‘Indigenous led’ yielded any results.
4 As outlined in the limitations section above, the findings of this report will be presented as proportions rather than total values in dollars.

The surges in locally led terminology seen in Figure 2 could reflect advances in policy at these times, for example, the 
agreement of the GBF in 2022, which included a strong emphasis on the role of IPs and LCs in advancing biodiversity 
action. Furthermore, the launch of the LLA principles in 2021 brought locally led terminology into more common use in 
both climate and nature policy spheres.
While the increase in the use of locally led terms (and by association, projects that can be inferred to be locally led) is 
greater than the increase in funding for local implementation, the overall amount of projects that reference locally led 
action still remains tiny in comparison. This finding is deeply concerning, as it indicates that even where money is spent at 
the local level or where there are benefits for IPs and LCs, over 99% of nature projects are still led by non-local actors; IPs 
and LCs who steward nature still lack decision-making power and agency over how funding is spent in their territories.
We also looked at the proportion of funding that was marked as ‘principal’ for biodiversity, rather than ‘significant’. The 
proportion for locally led biodiversity action marked as principal was 81.3%, much higher than for funding that targets 
the local level (58.3%) or total nature finance (59.8%). As outlined in the methods section above, projects should 
be marked as ‘principal’ against the biodiversity marker if the main purpose of the funding is to provide biodiversity 
benefits. The OECD suggests that the following question provides a good guide for how to apply the markers: Would 
the activity have been undertaken without this objective? (OECD, 2024c). If biodiversity is the main objective, it should 
be marked as ‘principal’; if biodiversity objectives are important to the funding, but are not one of the principal reasons 
for undertaking the activity, it should be marked as ‘significant’. Otherwise, it should be marked as ‘not targeted’. So 
these figures show that funding that uses locally led terminology is much more likely to be marked as principally about 
biodiversity than funding that is not locally led.
There is also a surprisingly high proportion of projects marked as ‘principal’ for biodiversity that are also marked as 
‘principal’ for the adaptation marker: 24% of local-level nature projects and 42% of locally led nature projects. This 
means that almost half of all the projects marked as locally led were reported to be explicitly about both nature and 
adaptation. While this may be evidence of the strong association between nature and adaptation actions as these 
are experienced on the ground, existing research suggests a tendency for ‘over-tagging’ of the Rio markers, whereby 
funders are inclined to report greater alignment with the markers than the reality (Weikmans et al., 2017; Wood and 
Leng, 2025), which may provide an alternative explanation.
All of the locally led disbursed funding was delivered using grants.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
  21
3.1.2 Nature finance to the local level
The proportion of nature finance targeting the local level (but not necessarily locally led) has been variable over time 
(see Figure 3). While the overall trend has been gently upward, there are large year-on-year differences and some 
backsliding over this timeframe. The overall upward trend in local-level funding allocation aligns closely with the 
welcome overall trend for increases in nature finance. While Figure 3 also shows clear yearly variations between both 
the commitment and disbursement data, there is no clear trend between commitments in one year and disbursements 
in the year or two that follow (as might be expected). However, the total proportion of nature finance with some local 
implementation is very close, with 33.7% of the disbursement funding and 32.2% for the commitment funding.
This is consistent with other studies that found that approximately 30% of GEF-7 biodiversity finance was targeted 
towards IPs and LCs (Sorsby et al., 2025). However, it differs from others, such as the OECD study that found that only 
8% of OECD DAC members’ biodiversity-related ODF was targeted towards IPs and LCs (OECD, forthcoming). This 
is likely because our study only looks at ODA, whereas the OECD study looked at ODF, which includes other types of 
finance, including non-concessional and private-sector finance. The overall upward trend is also consistent with the 
Path to Scale funding dashboard (Path to Scale, no date), which shows an approximate increase of US$500 million in 
total funding for IP, LC and Afro-descendant Peoples’ tenure rights between 2011 and 2024. Our finding is also similar 
to that of Treichel et al. (2025), which found that approximately 29% of total reported climate finance included some 
reference to local implementation.
Despite these positive indications, the results reveal that over 70% of all funding for biodiversity is not targeted 
towards the local level at all. Given the critical importance of actions by local actors such as IPs and LCs in protecting 
and restoring biodiversity, this finding is concerning. Furthermore, there is no way to determine whether the funding 
corresponding to the projects that referred to local implementation actually reached local actors or organisations 
directly, or whether it was just directed at the local level by a national or international intermediary organisation and 
included an indirect benefit for local actors. In many cases, funders rely on intermediary organisations to build trust 
with local actors and take accountability for ensuring that funding reaches the local level. Implementation of funds via 
intermediaries in this way may account for why so little nature finance appears to reach the local level. Funders should 
be more transparent about their use of intermediaries and the roles they play, including whether or not they absorb 
funds that would otherwise go to local actors. Additional research to trace and track nature finance allocations from the 
recipient perspective to shed light on the role and degree of the use of intermediaries would be enormously valuable.
In summary, the total funding that includes a reference to local implementation does not necessarily mean that the 
funding reached, or even engaged, local actors. Furthermore, this locally implemented funding should not be conflated 
with funding that is locally led; locally led funding not only reaches local actors, but they are playing a leading role in the 
design, implementation, decision making and governance of funded nature projects.

3.1.3 Frequency of ‘local level’ keywords
In terms of the most commonly used ‘local’ search terms, ‘communit*’ was by far the most commonly used keyword, used 
in 10.24% of total nature finance. ‘Local’ (9.47%), ‘rural’ (7.15%) and ‘farmer’ (2.88%) were the next three most common. 
Note again that each funding line may contain more than one keyword, so these percentages cannot be added together.
Comparison of highest frequency word use with highest funding amounts shows that although the top four keywords 
remain consistent regardless of which metric is used, for other words, there is considerable variation. For example, 
‘provinc*’ is the keyword with the fifth highest amount of nature finance, but is only the eleventh most frequently 
used keyword overall. ‘City’ is the eighth highest in terms of the amount of nature finance, but is not in the top ten for 
frequency of use — it drops to sixteenth for both total number of matches and number of individual funding lines in 
which the word appears (a keyword may be used multiple times in any individual funding line). This suggests that for 
both of these keywords — ‘city’ and ‘provinc*’ — they are included in funding lines with higher value than the average. 
On the other hand, ‘Indigen*’ ranks more highly for keyword frequency (fifth in terms of both total matches and the total 
number of individual funding lines that it appears in) than it does for total amount of funding including this keyword 
(where it is seventh), suggesting this keyword is included in projects worth lower funding amounts. See the tables in 
Appendix 2 for details.
3.1.4 Nature finance to Indigenous Peoples
Finance that explicitly mentioned IPs was extremely limited. Funding lines that included the individual term ‘Indigen*’ 
received only 2.02% of all nature finance, while only 2.24% included any of the Indigenous-related keywords (for 
example, the French or Spanish equivalents).5 This is much higher than the occurrence of the term ‘Indigenous’ in the 
climate data, which was found to be only 0.7% (Treichel et al., 2025). While this is unsurprising, given the stronger 
emphasis on the role of IPs in nature policy and practice, it is still shockingly low in both cases.
Funding focused on IPs has generally increased over time, both absolutely and as a proportion of total nature finance, 
with the trend increasing since 2019 (see Figure 4). However, even in the highest year, less than 5% of all nature 
finance made any mention of the word Indigenous or any of the many related keywords we searched for across the 
three languages.

Furthermore, the term ‘Indigenous led’ was only found a handful of times in the data from 2019 to 2024, with the terms 
‘locally led’ and ‘community led’ much more frequently used. The tiny fraction of projects found to include ‘Indigenous 
led’ as a search term indicates that IPs’ leadership is still barely recognised in nature finance, with the vast majority of 
finance implemented with IPs still designed and led externally.
We acknowledge that neither ‘locally led’ nor ‘Indigenous led’ terms are able to fully capture the essence of what IPs 
have been asking for from international nature finance policy, which is for finance to support projects that are needed 
and wanted by communities, in line with their self-determined needs and priorities. Our analysis is not able to offer 
further insight into the extent to which projects are in line with the self-determined priorities of IPs and LCs; we use the 
‘Indigenous led’ search term only as a proxy indicator to suggest how many projects may be being led by IPs, in line with 
the definitions described in Box 4.
3.1.5 Nature finance to (rural and) urban areas
The most frequently used of the urban-focused keywords were ‘city’ (1.8%), ‘municipal’ (1.42%) and ‘urban’ (1.24%). 
In total, urban synonyms were included in 5.82% of total nature finance.6 Of that, 0.36% (or 0.02% of the total nature 
finance) is for those living in informal settlements or slums.7 Urban keywords were in reasonably common use, but were 
out-used considerably by ‘rural’ and ‘farmer’ (see Section 3.1.3) as well as ‘fisher’ (2.18%), with ‘smallholder’ also used 
in 1.49%. In total, rural keywords were included in 13.5% of total nature finance.8 This keyword frequency suggests 
(perhaps unsurprisingly) that nature finance has a much greater focus on rural areas and actors than urban areas.
This supports the observation that urban areas are not prioritised for nature finance and the misconception that cities are 
not important hotspots for biodiversity (Oke et al., 2021; Malcolm-McKay and Lucero, 2024; Ives et al., 2016). Funding 
for nature in cities is often directed towards nature-based solutions as measures to adapt to or mitigate climate impacts. 
However, nature investment in cities and urban planning should also focus on biodiversity conservation and restoration, 
given that urbanisation is a major driver of biodiversity loss (Li et al., 2022; Simkin et al., 2022). Our findings support the 
argument that more nature finance should be directed towards urban areas. Even nature-based solutions are underfunded 
in cities, with less than 0.3% of spending on urban infrastructure going to nature-based solutions in 2020 (UNEP, 2023b).
The dominance of ‘rural’ in the current nature finance data differs from the climate finance data studied by Treichel et al. 
in 2025; they found a much more even split between ‘rural’ and ‘urban’ for climate change. This suggests that there is 
a greater focus on urban areas in climate finance than in nature finance. Also significant is that despite the relatively 
low occurrence of ‘urban’ and related keywords, they are still used almost three times more frequently than the term 
‘Indigenous’ and related keywords (2.24% for ‘Indigenous’ and related keywords and 5.82% for ‘urban’ and related 
keywords). Given how much more prominent the role of IPs is in nature policy and the relative marginalisation of urban 
issues, this finding is surprising and further reiterates that not nearly enough biodiversity finance is reaching IPs.
Finally, the amount of nature finance reaching slums or informal settlements is surprisingly small (0.02% of total nature 
finance) and only a fraction of the total nature finance targeting urban areas more broadly (5.82%). This could indicate 
that more nature finance which is reaching cities is going to urban greening projects in more affluent areas rather 
than to the most vulnerable people, who are more likely to rely directly on nature and natural resources to meet their 
basic needs. Further research would be needed to test this hypothesis, but what is clear is that the proportion of nature 
finance targeting cities’ most vulnerable residents is incredibly low.

3.2 How nature finance is provided
3.2.1 Commitment versus disbursement data
As outlined in Section 2.1, in this report, we examine disbursement data rather than commitment data — that is, we 
look at how much money OECD DAC members actually gave to countries in a given year, rather than how much they 
committed to countries in that year. Here, we offer a reflection on the trends between commitment and disbursement 
data. In general, the commitment figures are higher than the disbursement figures, but follow the same broad trends 
in terms of the proportion targeting local and Indigenous nature actors or for locally or Indigenous-led nature action. 
Overall, of the finance reported by OECD DAC members between 2011 and 2024 tagged for biodiversity, we found 
that 32.2% of funding committed is targeting the local level compared to 33.7% for disbursed funding, and 0.28% of 
funding committed is locally led compared to 0.31% for disbursed funding. (See also figures 2 and 3.)
On average, the disbursement figures are only 83.5% of the commitment figures for all nature finance, while for nature 
finance with any ‘local’ keywords this proportion was marginally higher at 87.5%. On the other hand, the contrast 
between commitment and disbursement data is greater for locally led nature finance than for local-level nature finance. 
Only 75.1% of the level of funding committed to locally led nature action was disbursed over the study period. This is 
likely the result of locally led nature action seeing increased prominence in recent years, alongside the development of 
the INA principles. Because of the natural lag time between commitments and disbursements, the (slightly) increased 
recent commitments for locally led nature action therefore outweigh the historically very small disbursement amounts.
However, it is clear from the nature finance data more broadly that funding recorded in the commitment data does not 
always lead to actual disbursements. As such, we believe disbursement data is more accurate for estimating funding 
flows to the local level. This also points towards a need for funders to more consistently follow through on their funding 
commitments.
3.2.2 Sources of funding
In the OECD DAC data that we used, the non-bilateral (in other words, non-country) funders are called multilaterals. 
This category includes multilateral development banks such as the World Bank, Asian Development Bank or 
Inter‑American Development Bank, as well as multilateral agencies like the Food and Agriculture Organization of the 
United Nations or the United Nations Development Programme, and funds such as the GEF or GCF. The overwhelming 
majority of the reported nature ODA targeting the local level was provided bilaterally (97.2%), with the rest provided by 
multilaterals. This is slightly higher than the 92.6% of total biodiversity finance provided bilaterally.
Note that the original CRS dataset also includes private philanthropies as funders. However, these funders were filtered 
out of our data during the third step outlined in the methodology, in which non-ODA sources were excluded. As outlined 
above, those steps mean that our research only considers ODA, which is distinct from ODF — ODF also includes 
things like private-sector instruments, non-concessional loans and other debt instruments that are not provided at rates 
concessional enough to be considered as development assistance. Because our research does not include these non-
concessional instruments, our findings in terms of the proportion of finance provided by multilateral development banks 
(who use non-concessional instruments more frequently than other funders) may differ from other research that looks 
at ODF (such as OECD, 2024a). For instance, while our dataset includes the International Development Agency (IDA) 
(the arm of the World Bank that provides grants and highly concessional loans to the world’s poorest countries), only 
including ODA means that no funding provided by the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (which 
aims to reduce poverty in middle-income and creditworthy low-income countries through loans, guarantees and related 
risk management products) is included in our dataset.
The largest funders of nature projects using these ‘locally led’ search terms stand out — the UK (funding 42%) and the 
US (funding 35%), followed by the Netherlands (6%) and Ireland (4%). The Netherlands and the US were also some of 
the earliest adopters of this terminology, describing activities or projects as community led in 2012. Note that the vast 
majority of US funding over 2011–2024 was provided via USAID, so the withdrawal of USAID funding in 2025 means 
that we can reasonably expect to see funding for locally led nature action plummet from 2025 onwards. Preliminary 
data on 2025 figures from the OECD DAC suggests that overall ODA has declined significantly from 2024 (OECD, 
2026), with many other funders also reducing their contributions. This can be expected to have a damaging impact on 
nature finance, including finance to the local level and that is Indigenous or locally led.

Only one funding line included the use of ‘community led’ (or any related search term) in 2011 — that was funded by 
Germany, who provided 1.4% of the total funding for locally led action over the study period. There was no obvious 
trend in the list of recipient countries.
These findings on the main sources of nature-focused ODA are significant as most policy attention for nature finance 
is geared towards the GEF as a key multilateral funder of biodiversity finance and the host of the GBFF. However, 
we found that only a fraction of biodiversity ODA is provided through the GEF and other multilateral funders. This is 
consistent with other studies from the OECD, which highlight that multilateral funds such as the GEF and GCF only 
account for around 7% of biodiversity-related development finance (OECD and Organisation internationale de la 
francophonie, 2026). While a focus on the GEF and other multilateral funders is important given their role in potentially 
channelling climate and biodiversity finance directly to local actors, this finding still points to a need to refocus attention 
more on reform of bilateral funding streams.
3.2.3 The GEF: a key funder of biodiversity action
The GEF provides 1.65% of all reported nature finance. This figure might seem low, given the prominence of the GEF 
in international discussions about nature finance and their role as hosts of the GBFF, but as noted above, only 7.4% of 
all nature ODA is provided by any multilateral agencies or banks. This means the GEF provides almost a quarter of all 
funding not provided by bilaterals, so it is a significant funder to study.
However, the GEF poses a particular methodological challenge to our research. It is clearly an important funder of 
biodiversity action, both through its regular programming and more recently through its management of the GBFF. 
However, GEF funding lines in the OECD DAC data typically contain little additional detail in the ‘long_description’ 
column besides the project title or a broad category such as ‘Biodiversity’ or ‘CC STAR Allocation: IPs’. This provides far 
less detail and far fewer words for our keyword search to find potential matches, with our search then relying largely on 
project titles. Put another way, it makes it near impossible to know whether such funding lines target the local level or 
are locally led. This highlights the limitations of the keyword search approach — the OECD DAC data is self-reported 
by funders and contributors can determine the level of detail they provide. So while the following results for the GEF 
reflect lower than average ‘local’, ‘locally led’ and ‘Indigenous led’ action within nature finance, until and unless the 
reported GEF funding lines contain more details, these findings can be expected to be underestimates and the degree 
of that inaccuracy is not known.
	
•	
In that context, our research found that 13% of all GEF nature finance targets the local level. This local-level 
funding from the GEF makes up only 0.63% of all local-level funding. Note that the time period covered by our 
research (2011–2024) takes into account projects falling within the GEF-5 to GEF-8 replenishment phases.
	
•	
Only 0.58% of all GEF nature finance uses any ‘Indigenous’ keywords and only three GEF projects in the 
biodiversity data use ‘locally led’ or its related terms. There is a much larger Life Amazon project to be funded by 
the GEF Trust Fund in the commitment data — this constitutes 9.9% of all of the locally led commitment funding 
over the period studied and so would have a large impact if implemented (and therefore disbursed).
	
•	
The majority of GEF nature finance is provided via the GEF Trust Fund (62.9%) and GEF (general) (36.1%). 
The GBFF has not yet recorded any funding as delivered (in other words, disbursed), but there is a small amount 
listed across three projects, all in the 2024 commitment data. The GBFF only began operating in 2023, so 
unfortunately it is too early to assess the impact of the GBFF on biodiversity or local-level funding using OECD 
DAC data. Reports from the GEF itself indicate that the GBFF has surpassed its target to get 20% of funding 
to IPs and LCs (GEF, 2026), but this data is not yet available through the OECD DAC and therefore cannot be 
verified through our analysis. Similarly, there is no way currently to assess whether this GBFF funding is locally 
led or Indigenous led, rather than just targeting IPs and LCs as project beneficiaries.
	
•	
Also of note is that the GEF Trust Fund has a very large amount of nature finance reported as committed in 2023 
and 2024 that is not yet reflected in disbursement data. If these commitments are realised, this would dramatically 
increase the amount of nature finance via the GEF: it would represent almost a four-fold increase in total nature 
finance and likewise for local-level nature finance from the GEF. However, the disbursement-to-commitment rate for 
the GEF is much lower than average, at only 25.2% across the total period, compared to more than 80% on average 
for all other sources of funding. This suggests that it is unlikely that these commitments will be realised in full.

Our findings reveal that less funding channelled through the GEF is targeted towards local actors than the overall trend 
in biodiversity finance and the number of projects targeting IPs is also lower than the average across the full portfolio of 
nature finance. This is especially concerning given the prominent role of the GEF in the CBD negotiations and policy, as 
hosts of the primary financial mechanism of the CBD, the GBFF. However, the very short descriptions provided by the GEF 
to the OECD means our findings for GEF funding — which are based on project descriptions and titles — are likely to be 
underestimates. More consistent reporting to OECD DAC by GEF and all other funders, including adding detail to the long 
descriptions, would be needed to determine more accurate comparisons between funders.
It also remains unclear whether the GBFF is performing differently to the wider GEF portfolio, since no GBFF funding 
has yet been reported to the OECD as disbursed. However, given the target to get 20% of funding from the GBFF to 
IPs and LCs, it will be important to observe a higher amount of estimated funding targeting local-level implementation 
and using synonyms for locally led.
No disbursement data has yet been recorded for the GEF-7 Inclusive Conservation Initiative, only commitment data, and 
no data at all is available for the GEF-8 Heart of Conservation Initiative.
3.2.4 Financial instruments for local-level nature finance
Just over 80% of nature finance targeting the local level over the study period was provided via grants, with the 
remaining 19.1% provided using debt instruments (loans or equity). This compares to 24.9% of total nature finance 
provided using debt — in other words, funding targeting the local level tends to use less debt than biodiversity finance in 
general. Both overall and for funding targeting the local level, use of debt is increasing, though year-on-year trends vary 
significantly (see figures 5 and 6).
