  27
Funding for urban areas was more likely to use debt instruments than rural- or Indigenous-focused projects, with 7.11% 
of nature finance using ‘urban’ keywords using either loans or equity and only 0.41% using ‘rural’ keywords and 0.13% 
using ‘Indigenous’ keywords. No funding that included ‘locally led’ keywords used debt instruments at all.
Bilateral funders were more likely to use grants than multilaterals. Bilaterals used debt in 18.4% of nature ODA 
targeting the local level and in 22.2% of all nature ODA. For multilaterals, these figures were 44.5% for nature finance 
targeting the local level and 59.8% for all nature finance. In both cases, debt use was lower for funding that involved 
any ‘local’ keywords.
Particular funders demonstrate a much higher preference for debt instruments for nature finance than others. For 
example, 97.9% of all debt provided by bilaterals for nature finance was provided by just four countries: Canada, France, 
Germany and Japan. Between them, these four countries are significant funders of biodiversity finance, providing 
44.2% of all bilateral funding for nature finance and 40.9% of all nature finance. However, almost half (49.1%) of all of 
the nature finance from these four countries is provided using debt and this proportion does not drop significantly for 
funding that includes any ‘local’ keywords (48.8%).
Within the multilaterals, the IDA (part of the World Bank, described in Section 3.2.2) is a significant funder of nature 
action, individually responsible for 5.03% of all reported nature finance in our dataset. IDA provided 82.5% of total 
nature finance via debt over the study period. While IDA’s use of debt was significantly lower for funding that included 
any ‘local’ keywords (57.6%), this was still higher than the average for other multilaterals (44.5%). Note that in our 
dataset, while the category ‘multilaterals’ does include the multilateral development banks, it only includes ODA finance 
(so will exclude non-concessional lending). This category also includes other international development agencies (which 
do not provide loans at all).
Use of debt instruments in both climate and biodiversity finance is contested as they risk increasing the debt burdens 
of countries or communities that may lack the ability to repay loans, and force debtors to spend limited income repaying 
debts instead of investing in adaptation or nature conservation programmes that would improve their resilience and reduce 
the need for additional interventions in future (Patel, 2022; Dempsey et al., 2021). While some studies show that credit 
and loan mechanisms that are designed and managed at the local level do bring positive benefits to local communities 
and help generate more finance to protect nature (Karlan et al., 2017; Adegbite et al., 2022), such instruments often 
go against the beliefs and values of IPs as they attach economic value to nature and treat it as a tradable commodity, 
rather than a living system (Sullivan, 2013; Barlow, 2024; Sorsby et al., 2026). In this context, the increasing use of debt 
instruments for nature finance is troubling. It is also evident that when debt instruments are used, more focus needs to 
be placed on ensuring these instruments can reach the local level and be locally led, and that they can be designed and 
implemented in ways that respect the rights and values of IPs.
3.3 How nature finance is counted: comparisons with 
other markers and common challenges 
3.3.1 Overlap with gender and other Rio markers
Of the nature finance that included related search terms for ‘locally led’, 76% were also marked with the OECD gender 
marker. While this is higher than the proportion of nature finance that targets the local level (of which only 61% was 
also marked with the gender marker), this means that almost a quarter of all biodiversity projects that are locally led are 
not tagged for gender, which is striking, given the explicit importance of gender in the INA principles.
In terms of the other Rio markers, only 10.9% of locally led funding tagged with the biodiversity marker had no other 
Rio marker tagged — in other words, almost 90% of locally led nature finance is tagged with more than one Rio marker. 
For local-level nature finance, this drops to 75.3%, while for nature finance more broadly, this is down to 61.6%. What 
this suggests is that nature finance that targets the local level, and especially that is locally led, is more likely to have 
co-benefits in the areas of the other Rio treaties than nature finance that does not.
In particular, 84.4% of the nature finance that included related search terms for locally led was also tagged with the 
climate adaptation marker, indicating a large degree of overlap between these two target areas. This was higher than for 
the markers for the other two Rio markers, with climate mitigation at 47.7% and desertification at 7.5%. In comparison, 
for biodiversity-tagged funding that targets the local level, 61.8% was also tagged for climate adaptation, 52% for climate

mitigation and 22.7% for desertification. In other words there is a much greater overlap between use of the adaptation 
and biodiversity markers for funding that includes locally led search terms than for funding that only includes local search 
terms. The overlap is similar for mitigation, but lower for desertification (for which far less funding is tagged overall).
3.3.2 High-level comparisons with the climate study
As outlined earlier in this report, our methodology and approach are adapted from that used by Treichel et al. in their 
2025 study to estimate flows of funding for climate action to the local level. Despite the similarities in our methodology, 
the two studies are not directly comparable due to the differences between the two datasets and the more extensive 
and refined list of keywords used in this study. Nonetheless, the general trends in proportions for local actors and locally 
led action can be observed to be broadly consistent across both studies.
Treichel et al. (2025) found that approximately 29% of total reported climate finance included some reference to local 
implementation, whereas the present study finds 33.7% of total reported biodiversity finance includes some reference 
to local implementation. The exact amounts reaching the local level are unknowable in both cases since it is impossible 
to trace the full flow of finance from donors all the way to the local level using the OECD DAC dataset; there are also 
insufficient tracking and reporting mechanisms in place by donors themselves. Treichel et al. (2025) found that only 0.17% 
of total reported climate finance includes a reference to locally led climate action, whereas the present study finds 0.28% 
of total reported biodiversity finance includes a reference to locally led action. The biodiversity figures are marginally higher 
in both cases than those for the climate data, but the impact of the differences in datasets and keyword lists may affect 
the degree of difference. Nevertheless, the similarity in the trend across both types of finance is clear.
3.3.3 Considering the distinction between nature and climate finance
In order to assess flows of finance for nature, it is necessary to consider nature finance as separate from climate 
finance; they are treated differently within the OECD DAC data, with ‘climate’ and ‘biodiversity’ projects tagged under 
separate Rio markers and the relevant datasets for tracking flows also distinct. This distinction is important in the 
international policy context, as it allows progress against the different goals set under each of the conventions, as well 
as holding funders to account on their financial commitments and ensuring funds are not double-counted.
However, the distinction between climate finance and nature finance is problematic for many local-level actors, especially 
IPs and other local communities directly impacted by nature loss and climate change. The impacts on the livelihoods, rights, 
culture and knowledge of these communities are not affected by how we classify the source or type of finance used to 
counter those impacts. Moreover, effective and appropriate responses to nature loss will help achieve broader development 
goals, such as helping to make communities more resilient to the impacts of climate change. This overlap at the local level 
is also reflected in the degree of overlap between the biodiversity and adaptation Rio markers for locally led funding. Such 
co-benefits are not limited to adaptation; nature is also critical for many mitigation efforts/actions, for example, through 
sustainable forest management and protecting peatlands or mangroves.
Separating climate and nature finance streams therefore matters for ‘upstream’ accounting discussions, but can be 
actively harmful for its effectiveness ‘downstream’. Focusing on how funding meets the needs of funders and their 
priorities (as determined by international metrics and markers) can lead projects to be designed with limited scope — 
for example, with only one Rio Convention ‘benefit’ in mind — without due regard for potential co-benefits and, in so 
doing, overlook easy additional wins. Worse, it can lead to the exclusion of the needs of key actors on the ground, in 
whose name such funding is provided in the first place. Efforts should be made in international policy to break down the 
siloes between nature and climate and streamline local-level finance for these issues under unified funding streams.

3.3.4 Using OECD DAC categories
While the OECD DAC provides the most extensive dataset for tracking flows of development aid finance, there are 
some shortcomings specific to tracking local flows (see Section 2.2 on limitations). Chief among these is the lack of an 
inbuilt indicator that distinguishes local from non-local flows.9
The OECD DAC data does include a category titled ‘channel of delivery’. This describes the initial recipient of funding 
— there may be other recipients further along the delivery chain, but this category reflects the first recipient to receive 
the reported funding. Unfortunately, this category doesn’t easily allow for tracking of local-level recipients. This is partly 
because local recipients may well not be the initial recipients of funding but are further along the funding chain, and 
also because the categories are not well suited to reflecting our definitions of ‘local’ (outlined in Box 4). For example, 
some categories (such as the one for universities and think tanks) do not distinguish between actors based in recipient 
countries and those in the funder countries. So this data is particularly limited in what it can reveal. The following 
categories would include local actors (though some would obviously also include local actors within funder countries, 
who we would exclude from our accounting):
	
•	
12002: local governments in recipient countries
	
•	
23000: developing country-based NGO
	
•	
30000, 31000 and 32000: public–private partnerships and networks
	
•	
51000: university, college, research institute or think-tank
	
•	
62000: private sector in recipient country
Funding channelled to this set of recipients — in other words, delivered directly to subnational actor types within both 
funder and recipient countries — accounted for only 6.6% of all reported nature finance. That does not align with our 
keyword search findings, which explore local actors based in recipient countries, for which this figure is 33.7%. Further, 
there was limited overlap between the funding lines found through these two approaches, with just under half of the 
funding lines using the above channel of delivery codes using any of our local keywords. This suggests that — despite 
their potential — the channel of delivery categories are not currently a useful mechanism for estimating flows to 
local actors. Treichel et al. (2025) similarly explored the channel of delivery as a means to explore first-order funding 
recipients and made recommendations for improving this reporting element to allow users to distinguish between 
funding recipients that are based in funder countries from funding recipients based in recipient countries, and thereby 
allow clearer analysis of funding flows. We reiterate those recommendations.
9 As outlined in Box 4, our definition of local differs from the OECD DAC’s in one important way: we consider ‘local’ to be sub-national and so exclude national 
governments from lists of local actors.

4	
 
Conclusions and 
recommendations
Our analysis reveals that only a tiny proportion of total reported nature finance is Indigenous or locally led. A lack of 
dedicated mechanisms to track funding to the local level limits the ability to accurately estimate total funding amounts 
for local actors; however, the keyword search approach reveals that proportions for local and Indigenous actors remain 
shockingly low. More efforts are needed to improve both the quantity and quality of nature finance for IPs and LCs.
Overall, the results of the study show that locally led finance for nature is still lagging far behind where it needs to be 
to meet global policy commitments and deliver on the LLA and INA principles, which are gaining increasing traction 
from local and international stakeholders in nature and climate finance policy negotiations. Not only does the quantity of 
nature finance going to IPs and LCs need to increase, but more attention also needs to be paid to ensuring that IPs and 
LCs lead throughout the design, implementation, decision making and governance of projects.
Furthermore, formal mechanisms to consistently track funding reaching the local level are lacking. There are currently 
no appropriate indicators for local-level engagement or processes to maintain transparency over funding flows within 
the key reporting frameworks for donors, such as the OECD DAC. Keyword search methodology, despite its many 
limitations, is therefore the best tool currently available for tracking these trends. Similarly, the OECD dataset and the 
Rio marker system remain the best available resources to monitor overall nature finance flows, despite their critiques. 
There is a clear need for more studies backed by on-the-ground data from funding recipients to complement the 
tracking that is done on data provided by the funders.
Based on these findings, we present the following recommendations for nature finance policymakers and funding 
bodies, as well as recommendations for further research. We urge parties to the CBD negotiations on resource 
mobilisation, financial mechanism and the monitoring framework to consider these recommendations and address them 
at CBD COP17 and beyond.
Recommendations on the quantity of nature finance:
	
•	
More finance for nature needs to reach the local level, and more needs to be locally led. Additionally, more 
finance for nature needs to reach IPs and be led by IPs. This is critically important given the unique role of IPs in 
conserving and restoring nature.
	
•	
Specific indicators should be introduced to the OECD DAC and other reporting frameworks, such as the GBF 
monitoring framework and GEF indicators applied to the GBFF, to accurately measure how much finance 
reaches local actors and how much is locally led. Within the OECD DAC reporting, a first step would be to 
expand the existing channel of delivery codes to allow subcategories to clearly distinguish between local funding 
recipients based in funder countries from those in recipient countries. In addition, funders should engage in 
substantive dialogue with IPs to assess the extent to which projects are in line with the priorities of IPs and to 
explore the development of appropriate tracking mechanisms.

pages.text:
CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
  31
	
•	
More finance for nature should be directed towards urban areas to fund nature-based solution projects and 
conserve natural biodiversity in cities. Further research is needed to determine why finance for nature in cities is 
not reaching the most vulnerable communities and slum dwellers.
Recommendations on how nature finance is delivered:
	
•	
Increases in commitments should theoretically result in increased disbursements, yet our data shows this is often 
not the case. As such, studies to estimate funding reaching end users should focus on disbursement data rather 
than commitment data.
	
•	
Moreover, each of the above recommendations highlights the importance of increasing the amount of finance 
reaching local actors — this should not mean merely increasing the use of local or locally led keywords in 
descriptions of finance, but for increases to translate to actual differences on the ground. To that end, future 
research should aim to compare nature finance contributions reported by funders to actual nature finance 
received by end-user recipients, both in terms of verifying the quantity of funding provided, and assessing the 
quality of finance and the lived experiences of communities and local people who receive it.
	
•	
The use of debt instruments for nature finance should be minimised. Where they are used, they should be 
designed in ways that ensure that the finance reaches the local level and can be locally led. They must respect 
the rights and values of IPs and LCs, with full adherence to self-determination and FPIC processes.
	
•	
International policy debates should pay greater attention to bilateral funding sources, which currently dominate 
the nature finance landscape — there is currently an over-reliance on the multilateral funds, especially the GEF, 
in nature finance policy discussions, which diminishes the responsibility of funder countries, especially in terms of 
the provision of grant/concessional finance for nature.
	
•	
Following the withdrawal of USAID funding, all funders should increase their focus on delivering more locally 
led finance for nature. This is now needed more than ever, and there is potential for small changes to have a 
significant impact.
	
•	
All funders, including the GEF, should improve reporting practices to the OECD DAC to be consistent and allow 
for cross-comparisons.
	
•	
The GEF, as the key multilateral funder channelling ODA to deliver the GBF targets, should focus on meeting the 
target of getting 20% of funds to IPs and LCs within the GBFF, and apply this across its wider funding portfolio.
Recommendations for both nature and climate finance:
	
•	
Funder countries should collectively agree upon consistent reporting approaches to ensure transparent and 
consistent tracking of their funding commitments. Efforts should be made to streamline this reporting to avoid 
double counting and reduce ‘over-tagging’ of projects using the Rio markers.
	
•	
Policy negotiations on finance within the UNFCCC and CBD should aim to break down the siloes between 
nature and climate finance, and streamline local-level finance for these issues under unified funding streams.
	
•	
OECD DAC members should update their CRS reporting system such that the ‘channel of delivery’ indicator 
could be used to track funding to the local level. This would rely on an appropriate definition of what counts as 
‘local’, which should exclude both regional and national-level actors.

Nature finance is essential to halt and reverse

affecting our planet. There is compelling evidence 
that nature is best conserved when it is managed by 
Indigenous Peoples and local communities, including 
local actors such as smallholder farmers, fishers 
and pastoralists. Local actors must therefore have 
leadership over how projects are implemented and 
funds are spent in their territories. However, evidence 
on how much nature finance is reaching the local level 
or is locally led is lacking. This report uses a keyword 
search methodology to explore trends in international 
nature finance flows and estimate how much is 
implemented with local actors, and how much is locally 
led. We also estimate how much of this finance is 
reaching Indigenous Peoples and is Indigenous led.

Abstract—Diabetes is a chronic metabolic disorder that affects 
millions of individuals worldwide and requires early detection to 
prevent severe health complications. This study presents a 
comprehensive Diabetes Health Prediction and Analysis system that 
leverages machine learning techniques to predict the likeli- hood of 
diabetes in patients. The proposed framework integrates data 
preprocessing, exploratory data analysis (EDA), feature engineering, 
and model development into a unified pipeline. Multiple classification 
algorithms, including Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and 
XGBoost, are trained and evaluated using standard performance 
metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. 
Experimental results demonstrate that ensemble-based models 
outperform traditional methods, with XGBoost achieving the highest 
accuracy of 91.76% and ROC-AUC of 98.41%. The system also 
includes a web-based application for real-time predic- tion, enhancing 
usability for practical healthcare scenarios. This work highlights the 
effectiveness of machine learning in medical diagnosis and provides a 
scalable solution for early diabetes detection and analysis.

I. INTRODUCTION 
Diabetes mellitus is one of the most prevalent non- 
communicable diseases globally, characterized by high blood 
glucose levels resulting from defects in insulin production or 
function. Early diagnosis plays a crucial role in managing 
the disease and reducing long-term complications such as 
cardiovascular diseases, kidney failure, and neuropathy. 
With the rapid growth of healthcare data, machine learning 
techniques have emerged as powerful tools for disease pre- 
diction and decision support. These techniques can identify 
hidden patterns in medical datasets, enabling accurate and effi- 
cient diagnosis. In this context, predictive modeling has gained 
significant importance in assisting healthcare professionals. 
This project presents a structured and end-to-end pipeline for 
diabetes prediction using machine learning. The workflow 
begins with data preprocessing to handle missing values and 
inconsistencies, followed by exploratory data analysis to 
understand feature distributions and correlations. Feature 
engineering techniques are then applied to enhance model 
performance. Multiple models, including Logistic Regression, 
Random Forest, and XGBoost, are trained and evaluated to 
identify the best-performing approach. 
Additionally, the system integrates a user-friendly web ap- 
plication that allows real-time predictions based on user input. 
The combination of analytical insights and predictive modeling 
makes this system a valuable tool for healthcare analysis and 
decision-making. 
II. RELATED WORK 
 
Machine learning in healthcare has evolved from basic 
statistical analysis to advanced predictive systems capable of 
early disease detection. Recent research focuses on improving 
prediction accuracy, feature optimization, and real-time clini- 
cal decision support. 
A. Machine Learning-Based Diabetes Prediction 
Early approaches for diabetes prediction relied on tradi- 
tional statistical models such as linear regression and ba- 
sic classification techniques, which often suffered from low 
accuracy and limited feature representation. Recent studies 
(2020–2025) employ advanced machine learning algorithms 
such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and 
XGBoost, achieving significantly higher accuracy levels 
(above 90%). Ensemble methods, in particular, have shown 
superior performance due to their ability to capture complex, 
non-linear relationships in medical data. 
B. Feature Engineering and Data Preprocessing 
Traditional models often used raw medical data without 
proper preprocessing, leading to poor generalization. Modern 
approaches emphasize: 
• Data Normalization: Standardization techniques to im- 
prove model convergence 
• Feature Selection: Removing irrelevant or redundant 
attributes 
• Feature Engineering (Our Approach): Creation of 
interaction features such as Age × BMI and polynomial 
features to capture hidden patterns 
These improvements significantly enhance predictive per- 
formance and model robustness. 
C. Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Models 
Most existing studies focus on single-model approaches, 
which may not provide optimal performance across diverse 
datasets.

• Logistic Regression: Simple and interpretable but limited 
in handling non-linear relationships 
• Random Forest: Provides better accuracy through en- 
semble learning but may increase computational cost 
• XGBoost (Our Approach): Offers superior performance 
with built-in regularization and gradient boosting, achiev- 
ing higher ROC-AUC scores and reduced overfitting 
Comparative analysis in recent literature confirms that en- 
semble models consistently outperform traditional classifiers in 
healthcare prediction tasks.

III. PROPOSED SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE 
 
The proposed system is a web-based intelligent healthcare 
platform designed for diabetes prediction, analysis, and recom- 
mendation. It consists of six core modules that work together to 
provide accurate predictions and user support. 
A. Data Input Module (User Interface) 
• User Interaction: The system provides a web-based 
interface where users input essential health parameters 
such as BMI, glucose level, blood pressure, and lifestyle- 
related attributes. 
• Validation Logic: Input validation ensures that all values 
fall within acceptable medical ranges, preventing erro- 
neous predictions and improving system reliability. 
B. Data Preprocessing Module 
• Data Cleaning: Missing values are handled using mean 
imputation, and categorical variables are encoded into 
numerical format. 
• Normalization: All numerical features are standardized 
using z-score normalization to ensure uniform scale across 
features. 
• Consistency: The same preprocessing pipeline is applied 
to both training and real-time user input data. 
C. Feature Engineering Module 
• Feature Creation: Interaction features such as Age × 
BMI are generated to capture combined effects of health 
indicators. 
• Polynomial Expansion: Degree-2 polynomial features 
are created to model non-linear relationships between 
variables. 
• Optimization: Feature selection ensures that only the 
most relevant attributes are used for prediction. 
D. Prediction Module (Machine Learning Models) 
• Model Integration: The system uses trained models 
including Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XG- 
Boost. 
• Decision Logic: Among these, XGBoost provides the fi- 
nal prediction due to its superior performance in accuracy 
and generalization. 
• Output: The model predicts: 
– Presence or absence of diabetes 
– Probability score for risk assessment 
E. Recommendation Module (Diet and Treatment) 
• Personalized Suggestions: Based on prediction results, 
the system provides: 
– Suitable diet plans 
– Lifestyle recommendations 
– Basic treatment guidelines 
• Health Optimization: Recommendations are tailored to 
improve patient outcomes and promote preventive health- 
care.

F. Chatbot Integration Module 
• Interactive Support: A chatbot is integrated into the 
system to assist users with: 
– Diabetes-related queries 
– Diet and treatment clarification 
– General health guidance 
• Real-Time Assistance: The chatbot provides instant re- 
sponses, enhancing user experience and accessibility. 
G. System Workflow 
The overall workflow of the system is as follows: 
1) User inputs health data through the interface 
2) Data is preprocessed and normalized 
3) Feature engineering enhances the dataset 
4) Machine learning model predicts diabetes status 
5) Results are displayed with probability scores 
6) Personalized recommendations are generated 
7) Chatbot assists users with further queries 
IV. METHODOLOGY 
 
The proposed system follows a multi-stage data-driven 
pipeline for real-time diabetes prediction and analysis. 
A. Data Acquisition 
The system collects patient health data either from a struc- 
tured dataset or through user input via a web interface. The 
input includes key medical parameters such as BMI, glucose 
level, blood pressure, and lifestyle-related attributes. 
B. Data Preprocessing 
The acquired data undergoes preprocessing to ensure quality 
and consistency. Missing values are handled using mean 
imputation, categorical variables are encoded into numerical 
format, and all numerical features are normalized using z-score 
standardization to maintain uniform scale. 
C. Feature Engineering 
To enhance predictive performance, new features are gen- 
erated. Interaction features such as Age × BMI are created 
to capture relationships between variables. Additionally, poly- 
nomial feature expansion (degree = 2) is applied to model non-
linear patterns in the data. 
D. Model Training (Machine Learning) 
Multiple supervised learning algorithms are trained using 
the processed dataset: 
• Logistic Regression for baseline performance 
• Random Forest for ensemble-based learning 
• XGBoost for optimized gradient boosting 
These models learn patterns from the training data to 
accurately classify diabetes risk. 
E. Prediction and Risk Assessment 
When a user provides input, the system applies the same 
preprocessing and feature engineering steps before feeding the 
data into the trained model. The model outputs: 
• Diabetes prediction (Yes/No) 
• Probability score indicating risk level 
F. Recommendation System 
Based on the prediction, the system generates personalized 
recommendations, including: 
• Diet plans 
• Lifestyle modifications 
• Basic treatment suggestions 
These recommendations aim to support preventive health- 
care and disease management. 
G. Chatbot Integration 
A chatbot module is integrated to provide real-time assis- 
tance. It helps users understand predictions, clarify doubts, and 
receive guidance on diabetes management. 
V. 
ALGORITHM 
 
The proposed system follows a structured sequence of steps 
for diabetes prediction and analysis: 
1) The system continuously collects user health data 
through a web-based interface, including parameters 
such as BMI, glucose level, blood pressure, and lifestyle 
factors. 
2) The input data undergoes preprocessing, including han- 
dling missing values, encoding categorical variables, and 
normalization using standard scaling techniques. 
3) The processed data is enhanced using feature engi- 
neering methods such as interaction features (e.g., Age 
× BMI) and polynomial feature generation to capture 
complex relationships. 
4) The trained machine learning model (Logistic Regres- 
sion, Random Forest, or XGBoost) analyzes the input 
data to predict whether the user has diabetes. 
5) If diabetes is detected, the system further evaluates the 
risk level and identifies the possible type of diabetes 
based on learned patterns. 
6) Based on the prediction results, the system generates 
personalized recommendations, including diet plans, 
lifestyle changes, and basic treatment guidelines. 
7) A chatbot module is activated to assist users in clari- 
fying doubts, providing health-related information, and 
improving user engagement. 
8) All predictions, recommendations, and interactions are 
displayed on the user dashboard, ensuring a smooth and 
user-friendly experience.
